source: Ioannidis (2005) Why most published research findings are false
finding: A Bayes model shows a claimed finding is more likely false than true when studies are small, effects small, many relationships are tested, designs are flexible, or the field is hot.
numbers: PPV = (1-b)R/(R-bR+a). A finding is more likely true only if (1-b)R > 0.05. Box example: R=1e-4, power 60%: PPV about 12e-4; with bias u=0.10: 4.4e-4. Ten independent teams, one hit: 1.5e-4. Adequately powered RCT with 50% prior: about 85%. Six corollaries.
quote: It can be proven that most claimed research findings are false.
limits: A model, not an empirical count. Values depend on assumed R and bias. A 2022 correction exists.
agent_relevance: G3: one pass on the data used to find a result is weak. Discovery with many tried options needs a held-out confirmation, and each extra independent check raises trust.

source: Errington et al. (2021) Investigating the replicability of preclinical cancer biology (Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology)
finding: Only 50 of 193 planned experiments (53 papers) could be completed. Replication effect sizes were far smaller than originals.
numbers: 193 experiments planned, 50 done (26%) from 23 papers; 158 effects (136 positive, 22 null). Median effect size 0.43 vs original 2.96 (85% smaller); smaller in 92% of cases (108/118). Positive effects: same direction 79% (108/136); significant same direction 43% (42/97); original ES inside replication 95% CI 18% (17/97); replication ES in prediction interval 58% (56/97); meta-analysis significant 62% (60/97). Majority of criteria met: positive 40% (39/97), null 80% (12/15), all 46% (51/112).
limits: Most experiments were blocked by missing protocol detail or data; the 50 done may be the easier ones. Prediction intervals are lenient when the original was near p=0.05. Null effects replicated more often.
agent_relevance: Replication shrinks effects, and the cheapest check (same direction) overstates success. For G3, require the held-out check to hit a pre-stated criterion, and expect the held-out effect to be smaller than the fitted one.

source: Errington et al. (2021) RP:CB moderators
finding: Five candidate moderators of replication success showed no consistent link: animal vs in-vitro work, contract research lab, academic core facility, materials shared by authors, quality of author clarifications.
numbers: 5 moderators tested; none consistently significant. Animal experiments (36 effects) replicated less, largely because their original effects were smaller (122 non-animal effects).
limits: Moderators were correlated with each other; low power for subgroup tests.
agent_relevance: Replication failure was not explained by who ran it or by author help here. Treat a failed held-out check as evidence about the claim, not as a bad checker.

source: Serra-Garcia & Gneezy (2021) Nonreplicable publications are cited more than replicable ones
finding: Papers that failed to replicate in three large projects were cited more than papers that replicated, and the gap did not shrink after the failed replication was published.
numbers: Replicating papers cited 153 times less on average than non-replicating (N=80, Poisson regression, Z=-3.47, p=0.001). Only 12% of post-replication citations of nonreplicable findings acknowledge the failure. Source projects: psychology 39% of experiments replicated vs 97% originals; economics 61% of 18; Nature/Science 62% of 21; replicated effects about 75% of original size, failed ones near 0%.
quote: Published papers that fail to replicate are cited more than those that replicate, even after the failure is published.
limits: Observational; citation counts also reflect interest. Difference not significantly different across the three projects; largest for Nature/Science. Authors suggest reviewers apply lower reproducibility standards to interesting results.
agent_relevance: Contradicted results persist in the literature. An agent that trusts claims by prominence or repetition inherits failed claims. G3: weigh a claim by its held-out record, not by how often it is repeated.

source: Cortes & Lawrence (2021) Inconsistency in conference peer review: revisiting the 2014 NeurIPS experiment
finding: Two independent committees reviewed the same 166 papers. They disagreed on a quarter of decisions, and only about half of accepted papers would be accepted by the other committee.
numbers: 1,678 submissions, about 170 duplicated, 166 completed. Disagreement 43 papers = 25.0%. Both accept 22, only C1 accept 21, only C2 accept 22, both reject 101. Of C1's 43 accepts, C2 accepted 22 (51%); of C2's 44, C1 accepted 22 (50%).
limits: One conference, one year, about 22.5% acceptance rate. Simulation attributes inconsistency to reviewer subjectivity.
agent_relevance: A single judge or single pass is a noisy gate. Supports G4 and G5: one model's verdict is a hint, and an independent second check changes outcomes in about 1 in 4 cases.

source: Beygelzimer et al. (2023) The NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment
finding: A repeat of the NeurIPS consistency experiment in 2021 found similar noise. Duplicate-reviewed papers got inconsistent accept/reject decisions about as often as in 2014.
numbers: 882 duplicated papers; 203 inconsistent = 23.0%; random-accept baseline at 22.7% acceptance would give 35.1%. Counting 'could be bumped' as consistent: 16.0%. 50.6% of accepted papers would be rejected by the other committee. Pearson correlation of average scores between committees 0.575 (initial) and 0.586 (final).
limits: Decisions are closer to random than to perfect agreement; field grew a lot with no clear change in noise.
agent_relevance: Agreement of two expert scorers is only moderate. Use code-run checks over opinion judges (G5).

source: Raff (2019) A step toward quantifying independently reproducible machine learning research
finding: One author tried to reimplement 255 ML papers from scratch without author code. About two thirds reproduced.
numbers: 255 papers (1984-2017); 162 (63.5%) reproduced, 93 not. Readability had the strongest link ('Excellent' papers always reproduced). Ten variables significant, including pseudo-code, hyper-parameters specified, compute needed. Authors replying to email: p=0.004. Year of publication not correlated with success.
limits: One reproducer; reproduced = at least 75% of claims within tolerance; papers chosen by his interest. Pineau 2021 cites from this study 85% reproduced when authors helped vs 4% when they did not reply (selection bias possible).
agent_relevance: Under-specified claims fail to replicate. Every claim our agent outputs should carry enough detail (inputs, code, seed) for a second run to check it.

source: Pineau et al. (2021) Improving reproducibility in machine learning research (NeurIPS 2019 program and ML Reproducibility Challenge)
finding: Checklist and code-submission policies at ML venues, and a reproducibility challenge, with uptake numbers.
numbers: 173 papers claimed for reproduction in the challenge (92% increase), 73 institutions. NeurIPS 2019: code submitted for 71.5% of submissions where authors reported code. Cites 2014 NeurIPS experiment: committees disagreed on 25.9% and on 57% of the accepted list at a 22.5% rate. Cites Baker 2016: over 70% of researchers failed to reproduce another's work, over 50% their own.
limits: Policy description, partly self-reported; code availability is not reproducibility.
agent_relevance: Checklists and shared code raise the base rate of checkable claims; the schema's code-checked operators play the same role.

source: Henderson et al. (2018) Deep reinforcement learning that matters
finding: Same algorithm, same settings, only the random seed varied, gave statistically different results. Reported gains in deep RL can be noise or implementation detail.
numbers: 10 trials split into two sets of 5 seeds: 2-sample t-test t = -9.09, p = 0.0016. Network size (400,300) vs (64,64): KL divergence of updates 33.52 times higher. Same algorithm across different codebases varies widely.
limits: A few environments and algorithms; five-trial averages were common practice.
agent_relevance: A single run is not evidence (G3, G4). Require multiple seeds or held-out items and report spread before calling a change an improvement; same for our own A/B tests of the scaffold.

source: Liang et al. (2024) Can large language models provide useful feedback on research papers? (Nature family and ICLR)
finding: GPT-4 review comments overlap with human review comments about as much as two human reviewers overlap with each other.
numbers: Nature journals: 57.55% of GPT-4 comments raised by at least one human reviewer; per reviewer overlap GPT-4/human 30.85% vs human/human 28.58%. ICLR (1,709 papers): 39.23% vs 35.25%; for rejected papers 43.80%. By journal 15.58% to 39.16%. User survey: 57.4% found feedback helpful/very helpful; 82.4% found it more beneficial than at least some human feedback.
limits: Overlap with humans is not accuracy. Comment matching F1 was 82.4%.
agent_relevance: Model critique finds about what a human finds, and humans overlap little with each other. A critic is a hint source, not a replication (G2, G5).

source: Thakkar et al. (2025) A large-scale randomized study of LLM feedback for peer review at ICLR 2025
finding: A review-feedback agent was shown to randomly chosen ICLR 2025 reviewers. About a quarter updated their review, and updated reviews were judged more informative.
numbers: 44,831 reviews; about 50% randomly selected; 18,946 (42.3%) received feedback; 26.6% of those updated, incorporating 12,222 suggestions; reviews +80 words on average; over 96% of generated feedback passed reliability tests; those who got feedback were more likely to change scores after rebuttal.
limits: Voluntary uptake; longer is not necessarily better; no ground truth on correctness of the revised reviews.
agent_relevance: Feedback that code-run reliability tests check before display, and that points at concrete weaknesses, changes behavior (G2 pattern).

source: Latona et al. (2024) The AI Review Lottery
finding: At least 15.8% of ICLR 2024 reviews were AI-assisted, and those reviews scored papers higher and raised acceptance odds for borderline papers.
numbers: 15.8% lower bound (GPTZero). In 53.4% of same-paper pairs with different scores the AI-assisted review scored higher (p=0.002; +14.4% relative). Matched study: borderline submissions with an AI-assisted review were 4.9 percentage points more likely accepted (p=0.024).
limits: Quasi-experimental; detector error; cannot separate how AI was used.
agent_relevance: LLM judges are more lenient than humans, in line with G5 (fluent text is favoured). A model's score must not be the pass criterion.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind expert review: LLM-generated ideas were rated more novel than expert ideas, but not more feasible.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition; 79 expert reviewers (72 had reviewed for major venues). Novelty: human 4.84, AI 5.64 (p<0.01), AI with human rerank 5.81. Excitement: AI higher (p<0.05). Feasibility: human 6.61, AI 6.34, not significant. 4,000 seed ideas, only about 5% non-duplicate. LLM self-evaluation unreliable.
limits: Single field and topic; novelty judged by review, not outcome.
agent_relevance: Judged novelty is not outcome. Pair with the execution study (next line). G8: judge by running.

source: Si, Hashimoto & Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap
finding: Experts executed random AI or human ideas. After execution the AI ideas lost their novelty edge, and rankings flipped on many metrics.
numbers: 43 experts, over 100 hours each, 4-page papers, blind review. Human ideas barely changed (novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052). AI ideas dropped novelty -1.049, excitement -1.760, effectiveness -1.879 (1-10 scale). Difference in drops significant, p<0.05 on all four metrics.
limits: Small number of projects per condition; one field; execution quality varies.
agent_relevance: Direct analog of replication: a claim judged before running loses value after running. Evidence for G3 and G8.

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench: evaluating AI's ability to replicate AI research
finding: Agents must rebuild code for 20 ICML 2024 papers and reproduce results. Agents score well below human experts.
numbers: 20 papers, 8,316 gradable outcomes, author-approved rubrics. Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) 21.0%. On a 3-paper subset ML PhDs (best of 3, 48 hours) 41.4% vs o1 26.6%. Code-Dev variant: o1 43.4%. Best LLM judge (o3-mini with scaffold) F1 0.83 on auxiliary evaluation.
limits: Rubric partial credit; the judge is an LLM; some tasks underspecified.
agent_relevance: Replication from a paper alone is hard for current agents. Our agent should not claim a replication it has not run end to end.

source: Siegel et al. (2024) CORE-Bench: computational reproducibility agent benchmark
finding: Benchmark of running published code to reproduce results. Best agent solved about a fifth of the hardest tasks.
numbers: Best agent 21% on hardest level, 60% on easiest (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini). Table of past human audits: 2022 ML challenge 18 of 28 fully reproducible; Hardwicke 2021 psychology 16 of 25; Collberg & Proebsting 2016 311 of 601; Trisovic 2022 1480 of 2000 R files; Gertler 2018 economics 128 of 203.
limits: Capsule tasks with runtime limit; the audit counts come from other studies, read from the paper's table (column meaning not fully verified).
agent_relevance: Computational reproducibility is limited for humans and agents; checks must be run, not assumed.

source: Xiang et al. (2025) SciReplicate-Bench
finding: LLM agents implementing algorithms from 2024 NLP papers pass test cases less than half the time; missing or inconsistent descriptions are the main barrier.
numbers: 100 tasks from 36 papers; best LLM with Sci-Reproducer reaches 39% execution accuracy.
limits: Algorithm-level units, not whole papers.
agent_relevance: Ambiguity in the source blocks replication; the agent should flag unspecified details instead of silently guessing.

source: Beel, Kan & Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist
finding: An independent test of an automated research system found weak novelty checks, failed experiments and hallucinated numbers.
numbers: 5 of 12 proposed experiments (42%) failed from coding errors; each iteration changed about 8% more characters; median 5 citations per paper, only 5 of 34 from 2020 or later; 57% of manuscripts had missing or misplaced figures; cost $6-$15 per paper, 3.5 human hours. Micro-batching for SGD wrongly judged novel.
limits: Small sample (7 manuscripts, 12 experiments), one system, one domain.
agent_relevance: The system cannot critically assess its own results; code-located revisions from real output (G2) and held-out checks (G3) are needed.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist
finding: Automated system writes papers and an LLM reviewer scores them against human scores.
numbers: Only a keyword search of the text was done; found the statement that an average accepted NeurIPS paper has a human score around 6.
limits: Not read in depth; reviewer-validity numbers not recorded.
agent_relevance: Using an LLM reviewer as a replication gate is untested for validity; do not use it as the only gate.

source: Open Science Collaboration (2015) Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
finding: 100 psychology studies replicated. About a third replicated by significance; mean effect size halved.
numbers: From memory, not opened: 97 of 100 originals significant; 36 of 100 replications significant; mean effect size 0.403 -> 0.197. Serra-Garcia (opened) gives 39% for this project.
limits: Not opened; verify before use. Gilbert et al. 2016 criticised the design.
agent_relevance: Baseline for how often a fitted result survives a fresh test (G3).

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science
finding: 21 experiments from Nature and Science 2010-2015 were replicated at higher power. About 62% replicated and effects were smaller.
numbers: Second-hand from Serra-Garcia (opened): 62% of 21 replicated; replicated effects about 75% of original size; failed ones near 0%. Economics 2016: 61% of 18.
limits: Primary page not opened (redirect).
agent_relevance: High-profile papers replicate no better than average; prominence is no evidence.

source: Begley & Ellis (2012) Raise standards for preclinical cancer research
finding: Industry team tried to confirm landmark preclinical cancer findings; the large majority failed.
numbers: From memory, not opened: 6 of 53 landmark studies confirmed (11%).
limits: Not opened; methods unpublished; Prinz 2011 reported about 20-25%.
agent_relevance: Pre-RP:CB estimate; treat as a hint.

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: variation in replicability across samples and settings
finding: 28 effects tested across many labs. About half replicated; differences between sites were small.
numbers: From memory, not opened: 14 of 28 effects replicated; smaller effects than originals; little heterogeneity across samples and settings.
limits: Not opened (fetch failed). Verify.
agent_relevance: Failed replications were not explained by site or culture moderators, so a failed held-out check should count against the claim.

source: Gundersen & Kjensmo (2018) State of the art: reproducibility in artificial intelligence
finding: Survey of 400 AI conference papers on documentation of method, data and experiment.
numbers: From memory, not opened: about 6% shared code and 30% shared test data.
limits: Not opened; figures from memory.
agent_relevance: Most AI claims lack the material to be checked, which is why G3 needs the agent's own held-out run.

source: Raff (2019) author contact and reproducibility
finding: Papers whose authors answered the reproducer's email were far more likely to reproduce. Reply rate was about half.
numbers: Authors reply rate 52% of papers contacted; 'Authors Reply' variable significant at p=0.004 in the feature test.
limits: Authors who knew their code worked may have been more willing to reply (selection). Correlational.
agent_relevance: Missing details are repaired by asking. In a scaffold, the 'ask' is a check run on real output (G2) and an explicit list of unspecified details.
